column4: The Montecito debris flows are split into two events based off of their seismic signals. "Montecito" represents the aggregate signal recorded at a distance from multiple debris flows in Montecito Creek, Oak Creek, San Ysidro Creek, Romero Creek and Buena Vista Creek. "Montecito subevent" represents the signal recorded at close distances (within ~240 m) of an individual debris flow that passed near the QAD seismic station that includes material from both Buena Vista Creek and Romero Creek. Total areas, volumes, and peak flow heights are taken from Table 5., Kean and others (2019). Crown and toe locations for Montecito were chosen near the center of the debris flows based off Fig. 1., Kean and others (2019). Location coordinates for Montecito subevent were chosen near the center of the debris flow channel adjacent to the QAD seismic station. Upstream drainage area was estimated using drainage area and percent burned at medium to high severity from Table 1., Kean and others (2019).

In the early hours of 9 January 2018, intense rain above Montecito, California (USA), triggered a series of debris flows from steep catchments in the Santa Ynez Mountains. These catchments had been burned three weeks earlier by the 1140 km2 Thomas fire. After exiting the mountain front, the debris flows traveled across a distance of 3 km down a series of alluvial fans developed primarily with residential construction (Fig. 1), killing 23 people, injuring at least 167 others, and damaging 408 homes -- Quote from Kean and others (2019).
